title: Finn — Find your line
typeface: SF Pro Display outlined from installed Apple fonts; editable SF Pro source retained in Figma.
asset_policy: Official Apple hardware bezels and SF Pro; actual Finn UI. User-authorized generated human film plates. Original sound design. No fabricated product claims.

slides.title: Finn
slides.subtitle: Find your line.
slides.composition: Black. Finn at 220pt, centered; tagline 48pt underneath. No logo or decoration.
slides.motion: Cinematic v2: purposeful typographic reveal
slides.speaker_notes: Think about your last workout. You probably remember how many repetitions you did. But what did you learn from them? Today, I want to show you Finn: a way to turn a set into a useful next step.

slides.title: What changed?
slides.composition: White. A single left-aligned question fills the central field.
slides.motion: Cinematic v2: purposeful typographic reveal
slides.speaker_notes: When we train alone, we can track time, weight and repetitions. Understanding the movement itself is harder. A camera can give us a different perspective. The challenge is turning what it sees into something clear enough to use on the next set. That is the question behind Finn.

slides.title: A new perspective.
slides.composition: Black. Oversized headline left, official silver iPhone right with actual Home capture.
slides.motion: Cinematic v2: shared device and extracted actual UI
slides.speaker_notes: Finn brings a camera-based training flow to iPhone. Choose a supported movement, set up the camera and begin. The experience is deliberately focused: help you capture a set, understand what was observed and decide what to do next. Let me take you through it.

slides.title: Choose. Frame. Move.
slides.composition: Black. Three words vertically left, large iPhone with recorded setup flow right.
slides.motion: Cinematic v2: shared device and extracted actual UI
slides.speaker_notes: We start with a movement. Finn gives framing guidance before the set begins. This matters because the quality of the view affects what the app can observe. You can begin manually, and the app also has a hands-free flow. For this presentation, the recording uses the app’s explicitly labelled synthetic demo input. It demonstrates the interaction, not a measured athlete or an accuracy claim.

slides.title: A tip. At the right moment.
slides.composition: Black. iPhone centered-right; headline left. Actual recording preserves DEMO INPUT.
slides.motion: Cinematic v2: shared device and extracted actual UI
slides.speaker_notes: This is where Finn becomes useful during the set. It follows the movement, counts repetitions, and can give a short posture cue when the evidence supports one. In this scripted example, the cue is “Sit lower.” It is brief enough to act on without reading a paragraph. The film illustrates that feedback loop; its generated actor is not a validation study.

slides.title: One useful observation.
slides.composition: White. Giant 1 left with short caption; result capture inside iPhone right.
slides.motion: Cinematic v2: shared device and extracted actual UI
slides.speaker_notes: The result is intentionally constrained. Finn reports at most one supported observation. It looks for a repeated pattern rather than reacting to a single isolated frame. If the evidence is insufficient, the result can say that a retake is needed, or that no supported pattern was found. No supported pattern is not a declaration of perfect form. This restraint is a central product decision: clarity should not come from pretending we know more than we do.

slides.title: Keep the insight.
slides.composition: Black. History and result device pair; small title in upper-left, no chart invented.
slides.motion: Cinematic v2: shared device and extracted actual UI
slides.speaker_notes: Each completed set becomes a local summary. History lets you revisit it. Compatible sets can be compared, and repeated observations can become easier to notice over time. This is the start of a feedback loop: capture, understand, try again. A useful observation should stay with you after you put the phone away. Finn gives that observation somewhere to live, so you can bring it into the next session.

slides.title: Six movements.
slides.subtitle: supported exercises
slides.composition: White. Large numeral 6 at left, two neat columns of exercise names right.
slides.motion: Cinematic v2: shared device and extracted actual UI
slides.speaker_notes: The current implementation supports six exercises: squat, push-up, static lunge, stiff-leg deadlift, pull-up and bar muscle-up. They do not all use the same interpretation. Some rely on a side view, while the bar movements use a shoulder-motion signal. That is why explicit movement selection and framing matter. We are starting with a defined scope.

slides.title: See the movement.
slides.composition: Black. Title left, actual Posture tab in iPhone right.
slides.motion: Cinematic v2: shared device and extracted actual UI
slides.speaker_notes: Before recording, the Posture area helps you explore the movements through illustrated loops and short guidance. These are movement illustrations, not reference measurements. It is a useful bridge from choosing an exercise to knowing how to set up. The experience can guide the user before the camera is even running.

slides.title: Your sets. In context.
slides.composition: Black. Coach screen on iPhone right; headline left.
slides.motion: Cinematic v2: shared device and extracted actual UI
slides.speaker_notes: Coach connects the conversation back to saved sets. In the on-device Foundation Models path, the model selects relevant saved sessions; the app builds the displayed answer from recorded facts. That separation is deliberate. Your repetition count and measurements remain tied to the recorded session. Ask about the last set, revisit an observation, or bring relevant context into the next workout. When the model is unavailable, a fixed response path keeps that context accessible.

slides.title: A little guidance. Right here.
slides.composition: Black. Official Watch prominent right, iPhone smaller left, minimal headline above.
slides.motion: Cinematic v2: shared device and extracted actual UI
slides.speaker_notes: Apple Watch brings that short line closer. The iPhone remains the camera and analysis device. WatchConnectivity carries the current set state and a concise coaching message to the wrist. The Watch can also provide an optional rhythm guide, with an interval chosen by the person. Those taps are pacing cues, not judgements of technique. If the phone disconnects, the Watch stops presenting stale coaching as live. Physical-device reliability remains part of the validation work.

slides.title: Closer.
slides.subtitle: Widgets   Live Activities   App Intents
slides.composition: White. Bold two-line headline; three Apple technology names below in a single sparse row.
slides.motion: Cinematic v2: shared device and extracted actual UI
slides.speaker_notes: Finn also has implementation for system entry points: widgets, Live Activities and App Intents. These bring a last-set summary or a quick action closer to the user. Start a set. Revisit the last one. Open your history. Each entry point connects back to the same training experience. The opportunity is a product that feels at home across the system, including the moments when the full app is not open.

slides.title: Built on Vision.
slides.subtitle: AVFoundation   →   Vision   →   Evidence   →   Feedback
slides.composition: Black. Four-stage horizontal pipeline as editable type and thin rules; title upper-left.
slides.motion: Cinematic v2: shared device and extracted actual UI
slides.speaker_notes: Underneath Finn is an Apple-native movement pipeline. AVFoundation supplies camera frames. Vision detects body landmarks on the device. Finn follows the selected athlete and converts those landmarks into joint geometry and movement over time. We sample analysis at up to fifteen frames per second. Before giving advice, evidence gates check whether the relevant body parts and camera view support that particular measurement. When they do not, Finn limits its feedback or asks for another view.

slides.title: Geometry becomes guidance.
slides.subtitle: AVFoundation   →   Vision   →   Evidence   →   Feedback
slides.composition: Black. Four-stage horizontal pipeline as editable type and thin rules; title upper-left.
slides.motion: Cinematic v2: shared device and extracted actual UI
slides.speaker_notes: The skeleton is only the beginning. Finn looks at angles, relative body positions and how those measurements change across a repetition. For a squat, one check compares the torso and shin angles near the bottom of the movement. A repeated chest drop can produce the short cue “Chest up.” Each check has its own required joints and confidence rules. The Watch relays that phone-authored message. The language model does not invent the biomechanics.

slides.title: A trained eye. Explicit rules.
slides.subtitle: AVFoundation   →   Vision   →   Evidence   →   Feedback
slides.composition: Black. Four-stage horizontal pipeline as editable type and thin rules; title upper-left.
slides.motion: Cinematic v2: shared device and extracted actual UI
slides.speaker_notes: How is it trained? The body-pose model is pretrained by Apple and supplied through Vision. We have not trained that model ourselves. Finn’s current exercise recognition and form checks use explicit rules on joint geometry and motion. Optional Create ML and Core ML classifier interfaces exist, but no custom trained classifier ships in this build. The next step is testing those rules on consented real movement, varied bodies, camera angles and lighting, rather than treating synthetic fixtures as evidence of accuracy.

slides.title: Apple Intelligence. Grounded in your sets.
slides.subtitle: Saved sets  →  Relevant context  →  Recorded facts
slides.composition: White. Large headline left; three-stage text stack right with Foundation Models as small label.
slides.motion: Cinematic v2: shared device and extracted actual UI
slides.speaker_notes: The coach uses Foundation Models, the Swift framework for Apple Intelligence. It receives a compact context made from saved set facts. Guided generation asks the model to select relevant set references in a structured response. Finn validates those references and presents the recorded facts, so a fluent answer cannot silently become a new measurement. The current implementation prefers Private Cloud Compute when available, then the on-device model. If neither can answer, it can still show saved observations. That is why we should describe the movement analysis as on-device, while explaining the coach’s actual routing separately.

slides.title: Zero workout videos saved.
slides.subtitle: workout videos saved
slides.composition: Black. Giant 0 centered, caption below. No padlock illustration or decorative badge.
slides.motion: Cinematic v2: purposeful typographic reveal
slides.speaker_notes: The camera is there to understand the set. Finn’s current capture pipeline processes the frames on device and does not save raw workout video. What persists is the local set summary. Optional Health integration has its own permission and validation requirements. The development recordings in this deck were deliberately captured for presentation; they are separate from the app’s normal workout storage behavior.

slides.title: One set. One insight. Another step.
slides.composition: Black. Three large lines, progressive emphasis with system pink only on insight.
slides.motion: Cinematic v2: shared device and extracted actual UI
slides.speaker_notes: That is the loop we are building. Make the set easy to capture. Make the observation easy to understand. Make it easy to return and see what happened next. The product is most useful when its information is small enough to remember and grounded enough to trust.

slides.title: Real-world reps.
slides.subtitle: Athletes. Trainers. Real devices.
slides.composition: White. Three short words beneath the headline; candid development milestone, no launch promise.
slides.motion: Cinematic v2: purposeful typographic reveal
slides.speaker_notes: The next step is real-world validation: varied athletes and environments, trainer review, and paired physical-device checks. Those are necessary before we can speak about accuracy or training outcomes. Today, what you have seen is the implemented experience and the principles guiding the next phase.

slides.title: Find your line.
slides.subtitle: Find your line.
slides.composition: Black. Same typography as opening; small final tagline.
slides.motion: Cinematic v2: purposeful typographic reveal
slides.speaker_notes: Finn. Find your line. Thank you.
